question: In the municipality of Planes (comarca of el Comtat, Autonomous Community of Valencia), the Modern Eco Village mega-development – comprising up to 500 luxury homes on rural land, next to the River Serpis and the Beniarrés reservoir – is going ahead in an area partially included in the Natura 2000 network.

The project could double or triple the local population and has prompted concerns about its environmental, water and public participation effects. In the light of Directive 2011/92/EU, the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) and the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC): 1.
Has the Commission received any information on Spain’s compliance with the environmental assessment requirements for this project?

Given the projected population increase (115 % – 215 %) in an area where water stress is a recurrent problem, does the Commission believe that Spain is complying with Article 4 of the Water Framework Directive, in particular the principle of nondeterioration, and has it checked the conduct of the Confederación Hidrográfica del Júcar (the Júcar river basin authority)?
What measures could the Commission take to help to secure effective public participation in line with the Aarhus Convention?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.11.2026) Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law of individual projects.

According to Article 6 (3) of the Habitats Directive1, projects likely to have a significant effect on Natura 2000 sites must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site in view of the site’s conservation objectives. It is for the competent national, regional and local authorities to ensure compliance with these provisions, if relevant in this case.

As regards the Water Framework Directive2, Member States are required to ensure that projects liable to affect water bodies do not cause deterioration of their status and do not compromise the achievement of the applicable environmental objectives, unless the conditions for an exemption laid down in the Directive are fulfilled.

Member States are required among others to ensure a balance between abstraction and recharge of groundwater. This assessment must take account of the characteristics and status of the water bodies concerned and of the pressures associated with the project, including water abstraction and wastewater discharges.

Public participation in environmental matters3 is an obligation for Member States, including ensuring that the public is consulted when all options are open in an effective manner4. The Commission contributes to the full implementation of these provisions by sharing good practices, promoting training of judges on EU law5 and publishing guidance6.
1 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and

flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 2 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, p. 1–73, as last amended by Directive (EU) 2026/805 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 March 2026, OJ L, 2026/805, 20.4.2026.

3 Directive 2003/35/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 May 2003 providing for public participation in respect of the drawing up of certain plans and programmes relating to the environment and amending with regard to public participation and access to justice Council Directives 85/337/EEC and 96/61/EC - Statement by the Commission, OJ L 156, 25.6.2003, pp. 17–25.

4 Articles 6 and 7 of the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) Convention on access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters (Aarhus Convention): https://environment.ec.europa.eu/law-and-governance/aarhus_en. 5 https://environment.ec.europa.
